e-3722.problem:
The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown below. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=1$ and $x=4.$ Given that $f'(x) = 0$ at both $A$ and $B,$ find the intervals where $f'(x)>0.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/1a8208a75b7df62a0c692e08f74509ecf1462e3ab1f8dd7eae85a56272abde48.png)
e-3722.worked_solution:
We have $f'(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then $f'(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then $f'(x)<0.$

The information about $f'(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,1) & 1 & (1,4) & 4 & (4,+\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f'(x)>0$ on the interval $(1,4).$

e-3728.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Decreasing Using Differentiation
e-3728.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 8x$ is strictly decreasing.
e-3728.worked_solution:
To find where $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, we need to solve the inequality $f'(x) < 0.$

Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+2x-8,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2x-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
3(x + 2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right) < 0,
$$

and the graph of $y=3(x+2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right)$ has roots at $x=-2$ and $x=\dfrac 4 3,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/14e4f6078b21d209082c548f7f5d064abeaa98ee737aff919d2f6efad7a317e8.png)

The graph is negative on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ between the roots, so we conclude that $f'(x) < 0$ on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right).$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right).$

We have f′(x)=0 at the critical points A and B. Note the following:

  • If f(x) is strictly increasing, then f′(x)>0.

x(−∞,−3)−3(−3,0)0(0,3)3(3,∞)f↗max↘no extr.↘min↗f′+0−0−0+

Therefore, f′(x)>0 on the intervals (−∞,−3) and (3,∞).

The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown above. The points $A,B,$ and $C$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=-3,$ $x=0,$ and $x=3.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $A,B,$ and $C,$ find the intervals where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,-3) & -3 & (-3,0) & 0 & (0,3) & 3 & (3,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{no extr.} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the intervals $(-\infty ,-3)$ and $(3,\infty ).$

Question 2

The graph of the continuous function y=f(x) is shown below. The points A and B lie on the curve and have x-coordinates x=0 and x=2. Given that f′(x)=0 at both A and B, find the intervals where f′(x)<0.

a
(0,2)
b
(−∞,0) only
c
(−∞,0) and (2,∞) only
d
(2,∞) only
e
No interval exists where f′(x)<0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We have f′(x)=0 at the critical points A and B. Note the following:

  • If f(x) is strictly increasing, then f′(x)>0.

  • If f(x) is strictly decreasing, then f′(x)<0.

The information about f′(x) can be summarized in the following table:

x(−∞,0)0(0,2)2(2,∞)f↗max↘min↗f′+0−0+

Therefore, f′(x)<0 on the interval (0,2).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms that f'(x) is negative only on (0,2), where the graph decreases. At x=0 and x=2 the derivative is zero, so both endpoints are excluded.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/269b71c2ec5653b6577e904a43374a45a0830f671850c7157a8d1bbfb49308f3.png)

The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown below. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=0$ and $x=2.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at both $A$ and $B,$ find the intervals where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$
content.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,0) & 0 & (0,2) & 2 & (2,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ on the interval $(0,2).$

after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $g(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =12{x}^{3}-24{x}^{2}+12x \\  & =12x({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =12x{(x-1)}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
12x{(x-1)}^{2}<0.
$$

Since $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for all real $x$, the sign of $12x{(x-1)}^{2}$ is determined by the sign of $12x$, so $12x{(x-1)}^{2}<0$ exactly when $12x<0.$ This yields

$$
\begin{aligned}12x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is restricted to $x\in (-8,8),$ we conclude that $g(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (-8,0).$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}$ is strictly decreasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)={e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2{x}^{2}-6x+3}(4x-6)<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to

$$
4x-6<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-6 & <0 \\ 4x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,\frac{3}{2}).$

after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=4{x}^{3}-27{x}^{2}-30x+9$ is strictly decreasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =12{x}^{2}-54x-30 \\  & =6(2{x}^{2}-9x-5),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
6(2{x}^{2}-9x-5)<0.
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
6(2x+1)(x-5)<0,
$$

and the graph of $y=6(2x+1)(x-5)$ has roots at $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=5,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/7eec3fc84b851b3b39e5ae8ecff1343f39393d1dd8f7a6cce8e8904dc1c65d48.png)

The graph is negative on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5)$ between the roots, so we conclude that ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5).$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\frac{1}{2},5).$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)$ is strictly decreasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 4x \\  & =\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{4x}{2{x}^{2}+1}<0.
$$

The function $2{x}^{2}+1$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
4x<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & <0 \\ x & <0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=5-7x-4{x}^{2}$ is strictly decreasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-7-8x \\  & =-8(x+\frac{7}{8}),\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
-8(x+\frac{7}{8})<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8(x+\frac{7}{8}) & <0 \\ 0 & <8(x+\frac{7}{8}) \\ 0 & <x+\frac{7}{8} \\ -\frac{7}{8} & <x.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (-\frac{7}{8},\infty ).$
